subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 8 periods = 320 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 5h 20min

periods.activity_title: Meeting the Old Stag: Read-Aloud and First Encounter

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Read (pp.43–46): teacher-led read-aloud of the full prose story with new words.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces new words from Let us Read (pp.43–46) — lush, stag, hillock, tender, sheltering, recovery — written on the board and briefly explained with a gesture or sketch.
Let us Read (pp.43–46): teacher reads the story aloud with expression, pausing after each paragraph to let students echo key phrases — "lush forest," "tender grass," "speedy recovery" — chorally.
Teacher re-reads the story a second time while students follow in their textbooks; students are invited to whisper-read along, matching the teacher's pace.
Whole-class oral recall: teacher asks two or three brief recall questions — Who lived on the hillock? What did the friends do when they visited? — and students answer in single sentences.

periods.teacher_notes: The story is adapted from The Panchatantra and carries a moral about shared natural resources; students who are familiar with Panchatantra tales will make quick connections. Ensure the new words — especially 'hillock' and 'lush' — are grounded in a quick sketch or gesture before the read-aloud begins, as these carry the setting's meaning.
materials: Blackboard or chart for new words

periods.activity_title: Thinking Through the Story: Comprehension Discussion

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think A (p.47): discuss and answer four short-answer questions on the story.

time_bands.activity: Teacher leads a quick shared re-read of the final two paragraphs of the story (pp.45–46) aloud, reminding students of the stag's recovery and the lesson the animals learned.

Let us Think A (p.47): teacher poses questions 1 and 2 — why was the stag popular, and why he could not go down the hillock — inviting pair discussion for a minute before students share answers aloud; teacher writes key phrases on the board.

Let us Think A (p.47): teacher poses questions 3 and 4 — why the green cover vanished, and what the animals did when they realised their mistake — students discuss in pairs, then volunteers share full-sentence answers with the class.
Class composes a single oral summary sentence for each of the four questions; teacher scribes these on the board as a shared model, and students read them back together.

periods.teacher_notes: A common difficulty here is conflating why the stag was ill (old age and illness) with why the grass vanished (the animals' greed) — keep these as two distinct ideas on the board. Students may need the prose passage re-read at the point of question 3; the specific cause-and-effect chain (visitors → grass eaten → stag weakens) is worth tracing sentence by sentence.

periods.activity_title: Speaking from the Heart: Discussion and Sharing Resources

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think B (p.47): guided class discussion — did animals do right, and resource sharing in nature.
Let us Speak (p.53): picture-based discussion on sharing a bowl of jalebis with classmates.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly recalls the story's ending: the animals felt ashamed, brought fresh leaves, and the stag recovered — students are asked to hold that moment in mind for the discussion.

Let us Think B (p.47): teacher poses question 1 — did the animals do the right thing in the end? — students take turns responding; teacher prompts students who disagree to explain why, keeping the discussion open.

Let us Think B (p.47): teacher poses question 2 — what would happen to green plants if everyone thought only of their own needs? — students share one-sentence responses; teacher draws a simple cause-effect chain on the board.
Let us Speak (p.53): teacher directs students to the jalebi picture on p.53; the four discussion questions are posed one by one, with students responding to each before moving to the next.

Teacher draws the two discussions together: the story's lesson — 'Nature has enough for everybody, but we need to use its resources wisely' — is read aloud together, and one student volunteers to say what it means in their own words.

periods.teacher_notes: The jalebi scenario on p.53 is a concrete bridge from the story's moral to students' lived experience; allow students to dramatise reactions briefly before asking them to answer formally. For question 1 in Let us Think B, accept both 'yes' and 'no' responses and ask students to give a reason — the aim is reasoned oral expression, not a single correct answer.

periods.activity_title: Meaning Makers: Matching Phrases and Descriptive Words

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn A (p.47): match five story phrases to their meanings.
Let us Learn B (p.48): identify descriptive words and sketch mental images for three noun phrases.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the five phrases from Let us Learn A (p.47) on the board — lush forest, tender grass, shaded spot, healthy food, speedy recovery — and asks students to predict meaning from context before the match is shown.

Let us Learn A (p.47): students draw lines in their textbooks matching each phrase to its meaning; teacher then goes through answers aloud, asking a student to read out each matched pair and use the phrase in a sentence.

Let us Learn B (p.48): teacher explains that descriptive words give more detail about scenes and objects, using the board phrase 'friendly animals' — students name what picture comes to mind; the idea of an adjective as a detail-painter is introduced informally.

Let us Learn B (p.48): students sketch in their exercise books the image that comes to mind for 'lush forest', 'tender grass', and 'healthy food'; pairs share and describe their sketch to each other in one sentence each.
Quick oral close: teacher asks three volunteers to say one descriptive phrase from the story and point to where it appears in the textbook, reinforcing the link between the words and the text.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes confuse 'matching meaning' with 'matching synonym' — make clear that the phrases carry the meaning of the whole noun group, not just the adjective alone. The sketching task in Let us Learn B is designed to be brief and expressive, not artistically judged; a simple doodle that prompts a descriptive sentence is the goal.

periods.activity_title: Adverbs of Manner: Noticing How Things Are Done

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn C (p.49): identify manner adverbs from a word table and write partner sentences for each.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the story sentence 'Each day, he warmly greeted his fellow animals and birds' on the board and asks: what does 'warmly' tell us about how the stag greeted? Students respond; teacher underlines 'warmly' and introduces the idea of adverbs of manner.

Teacher reads two more examples from Let us Learn C (p.49) — 'The old stag slowly recovered' and 'The rabbit quickly ate the carrots' — students identify the manner adverb in each and say what the action is; class composes one more oral example together.

Let us Learn C (p.49): students open textbooks and circle the manner adverbs from the word table — soon, badly, lately, cheerfully, quietly, early, carefully, highly, fast, regularly, nearby, loudly — teacher circulates and confirms as students work.

Let us Learn C (p.49): pairs write one sentence for each circled adverb in their exercise books; teacher moves through the class listening to pairs read their sentences aloud and prompts revision where the adverb is used as an adjective by mistake.
Three pairs share one sentence each; class evaluates together — does the adverb describe how, or something else? — and teacher names the manner adverbs confirmed.

periods.teacher_notes: A common confusion at this level is using 'early' and 'nearby' as adverbs of time and place rather than manner; accept these gracefully and distinguish them from the target set without labelling the error. Students build on their familiarity with descriptive words from the matching activity to notice that adverbs add detail to verbs the same way adjectives add detail to nouns.

periods.activity_title: The Monkeys' Fast: Writing Comic Dialogue

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write A (pp.50–51): fill speech blurbs in the six-panel monkey comic story.

time_bands.activity: Teacher describes the six-panel picture comic from Let us Write A (pp.50–51) — monkey king declares a fast, monkeys agree, collect bananas, feel tempted, break the fast, and conclude — students look at the pictures and predict what the monkeys might be saying in each panel.

Teacher models writing a dialogue for panel 1 on the board — the monkey king's declaration — thinking aloud about what the character might say and how to make it sound like speech; students suggest words and the class agrees on a final version.

Let us Write A (pp.50–51): students independently write dialogues in the speech blurbs of panels 2 through 6, referring to the pictures; teacher circulates and offers prompts — 'what is this monkey feeling here?' or 'how would she say that in one short line?'
Pairs exchange textbooks and read each other's dialogues aloud as a mini read-through; they check that each bubble matches what the picture shows and suggest one revision if needed.
Two students read their version of the final panel aloud; teacher points to how the conclusion — 'maybe fasting takes more self-control than we thought' — echoes the story's theme of self-restraint.

periods.teacher_notes: The comic task echoes the story's theme of temptation and self-control, giving students a playful way to revisit ideas from the prose. At this level, dialogues in speech bubbles should be brief and expressive — one or two lines per bubble; discourage students from writing lengthy explanations where a short exclamation or question works better.

periods.activity_title: Writing About My Best Friend: Guided Paragraph

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write B: fill and complete the guided paragraph about a best friend.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the paragraph frame from Let us Write B aloud, pausing at each blank and asking students to whisper what they might write; a quick show of hands reveals how varied the answers are, building interest.
Teacher models completing two or three blanks on the board with details about an imaginary friend — name, age, class, family — thinking aloud about choosing precise words rather than vague ones.

Let us Write B: students complete the full paragraph in their exercise books, filling every blank with details about their own best friend; teacher circulates, prompting students who are stuck on the hobbies or ambition blanks with brief questions.
Students read their completed paragraph to a partner; the partner listens and names one detail that sounded vivid or interesting, giving warm oral feedback.

Three volunteers read their paragraph aloud to the class; teacher highlights one strong sentence from each — especially the closing 'because' clause — and notes how giving a reason makes the writing more convincing.

periods.teacher_notes: This guided paragraph bridges the story's theme of friendship and loyalty to students' personal experience — the closing 'because' clause is worth special attention as it asks students to articulate a reason, a higher-order writing move. Ensure that the sharing step is kept warm and low-stakes; the goal is confident oral reading of their own writing, not a polished performance.

periods.activity_title: Thank You, Friends: The Old Stag's Card

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do (p.54): create a thank-you card from the stag — draw and write a gratitude message.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the card-making instructions from Let us Do (p.54) aloud and shows the illustration of the stag surrounded by forest animals; students are asked: what might the old stag most want to say to the animals who brought him fresh leaves?
Students fold a sheet of paper to make a card; on the front they draw the old stag surrounded by at least two or three of his forest friends, using the illustration on p.54 as a reference.

Students open the card and write a thank-you message inside — from the stag's perspective — expressing how the friends' help made him feel; teacher circulates and prompts students who are unsure with questions like 'how did the stag feel when the grass grew back?' or 'what do you say to someone who helped you?'

Gallery moment: students place their cards on their desks and walk around to read two peers' messages; each student leaves a small tick or a smiley on a card whose message they found especially warm or creative.
Teacher closes by reading the story's lesson — 'Nature has enough for everybody, but we need to use its resources wisely' — and asks one student to say how the thank-you card connects to that lesson.

periods.teacher_notes: The card connects gratitude, friendship, and the story's environmental lesson in a single expressive act; students who drew animals accurately and wrote heartfelt messages should both be celebrated. Encourage students to use at least one manner adverb in their written message — a natural bridge to the adverb work explored earlier in the chapter.

items.source_context: Old stag's popularity, illness on hillock, animals' greed depleting grass, and eventual recovery.
items.item_stem: Read the sentences below and mark each one True or False. Give one reason from the story for each answer.

options.text: After the animals stopped eating the grass, the stag slowly recovered.
The animals visited the stag because they cared about his health.
The grass on the hillock disappeared because of heavy rain.
The old stag lived in a valley near a river.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1 — False: the stag lived on a hillock, not a valley. 2 — True: friends visited to wish him a speedy recovery. 3 — False: the grass vanished because visiting animals greedily ate it. 4 — True: after the animals stopped and brought fresh leaves, and after good rains, the stag recovered.

items.source_lo: Student retrieves and infers information using a prose narrative as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Old stag's popularity, illness on hillock, animals' greed depleting grass, and eventual recovery.
items.item_stem: The animals in the story felt ashamed when they realised what they had done. In two or three sentences, explain what they had done wrong and what they did to make things right.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The animals had greedily eaten the tender grass on the stag's hillock while visiting him, leaving him with no food to eat even though he was ill. When they realised their mistake they stopped eating the grass and some of them brought fresh leaves for the stag instead.

items.item_stem: Look at the picture on Textbook page 53 showing four children around a large bowl of jalebis. Choose the best answer.

options.label: A
options.text: Each child should grab as many jalebis as possible before the bowl is empty.

options.label: B
options.text: Only the child who brought the jalebis should decide who eats.

options.label: C
options.text: The children should leave the jalebis untouched so they do not run out.

options.label: D
options.text: The children should share the jalebis so that everyone gets a fair portion.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Suggests the student has not connected the jalebi scenario to the story's lesson about greed.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Reveals a focus on ownership rather than the fairness and sharing the discussion targets.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Shows the student equates resource protection with not using resources at all, missing the idea of wise use.

items.item_stem: At the end of the story the animals learn: 'Nature has enough for everybody, but we need to use its resources wisely.' Speak for a minute: do you think the animals did the right thing in the end? Say what they did and give a reason for your answer.

expected_elements: Names at least one corrective action the animals took.
Gives a reason linked to fairness or care.
Connects animal action to the story's lesson.

items.item_stem: Write one line of dialogue for the monkey king at the moment he decides to declare a fast. The line should make clear what the monkey king wants the other monkeys to do.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Accept any line where the monkey king announces a fast — for example: 'From today, we shall eat nothing until sunset!' — as long as it is written as speech and states the fast clearly.

expected_elements: Names the friend and includes one personal detail.
Describes a hobby or activity the friend enjoys.
Gives a clear reason the friend is special.

items.visual_stimulus:
Phrase | Meaning
Lush forest | Quick healing
Tender grass | Nourishing, wholesome food
Shaded spot | Green and dense woods
Healthy food | Cool resting place
Speedy recovery | Delicate, young grass

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Lush forest – green and dense woods; tender grass – delicate, young grass; shaded spot – cool resting place; healthy food – nourishing, wholesome food; speedy recovery – quick healing.

items.item_stem:
Choose one manner adverb from the box and use it in a sentence about an animal from the story. Your sentence must show clearly how the adverb describes the action.

Box: slowly   cheerfully   quietly   carefully   loudly

expected_elements: Names one animal from the story.
Uses the chosen adverb to describe an action.
Sentence clearly shows how the action is done.

items.item_stem: Match each feeling or action on the left with the character or event from the story that best fits it on the right.
items.visual_stimulus:
Feeling or action | Character or event
Felt grateful after recovering | The visiting animals
Felt ashamed of their greed | The stag's hillock
Lost its green cover slowly | Fresh leaves brought as a gift
A kind act to help the sick stag | The old stag

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Felt grateful after recovering – the old stag; felt ashamed of their greed – the visiting animals; lost its green cover slowly – the stag's hillock; a kind act to help the sick stag – fresh leaves brought as a gift.

answer_key.left: A kind act to help the sick stag
answer_key.right: Fresh leaves brought as a gift

items.source_context: Stag's gratitude to forest friends; friendship and environmental care themes from the story.
items.item_stem: Imagine you are the old stag. Make a thank-you card for your forest friends. On the front, draw a picture of yourself with two or three of your animal friends. Inside the card, write two sentences thanking them for the help they gave you when you were ill.

expected_elements: Front shows stag with at least two forest animals.
Written message thanks friends for specific help.
Message is written from the stag's point of view.
